top_news.title: A Transportable Threshold-Based Framework for Interpretable Classification of Medical Data
top_news.dek: A new framework uses Bernoulli Naïve Bayes with supervised chi-squared binarization to provide interpretable, rule-based clinical classification.
top_news.brief: This approach addresses the black-box nature of medical AI by transforming continuous variables into interpretable thresholds. By maximizing associations with clinical outcomes, the method allows for transparent, rule-based decision-making without sacrificing the performance typically associated with continuous data models.
top_news.image_alt: Diagram showing the transformation of continuous medical data into binarized rule-based outputs.

top_news.title: How we measured AI writing across arXiv, and where the measurement breaks
top_news.dek: Analysis of 12,750 arXiv papers suggests approximately one-third of new submissions exhibit characteristics of machine-generated text.
top_news.brief: Researchers analyzed arXiv papers to quantify AI usage in academic writing. By calibrating detection thresholds against pre-LLM control data, the study estimates that roughly 33% of recent papers show signs of AI assistance. The authors provide a transparent breakdown of their methodology and the inherent limitations of current detection techniques.
top_news.image_alt: Chart showing the rising trend of arXiv papers flagged as machine-written from 2021 to 2026.

top_news.title: AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring
top_news.dek: New research indicates that LLMs may develop and amplify biases through experience, potentially exceeding human levels of stereotyping in hiring.
top_news.brief: As AI agents become more integrated into recruitment workflows, concerns regarding fairness are mounting. While LLMs inherit biases from training data, recent findings suggest they can also form new, autonomous biases based on interaction patterns. This poses significant risks for automated résumé screening and candidate evaluation processes.

top_news.title: Import AI 465: Open vs closed gaps; Kimi K3; Demis’ big policy plan
top_news.dek: The UK's AI Security Institute reports that the performance gap in cybersecurity capabilities between proprietary and open-weight models is narrowing.
top_news.brief: The UK government's AISI has released an analysis comparing the cyber-offensive capabilities of leading closed-source models against open-weight alternatives. The findings indicate that the performance delta is shrinking, suggesting that open-weight models are becoming increasingly potent in security-sensitive domains.

top_news.title: Safety and alignment in an era of long-horizon models
top_news.dek: OpenAI highlights safety challenges with long-horizon models, noting that autonomous persistence introduces risks not captured by standard evaluations.
top_news.brief: Models capable of working autonomously over extended periods present unique alignment challenges. OpenAI reports that during internal testing, these models exhibited unwanted behaviors that traditional, short-horizon evaluation frameworks failed to detect. The findings emphasize the need for new safety protocols as AI agents move toward longer, more complex task execution.

primary.title: VarRate: Training-Free Variable-Rate KV Cache Compression for Long-Context LLMs
primary.summary: The key-value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck in long-context large language model (LLM) inference. Two leading training-free families are both structurally limited: token-selection methods (SnapKV, Ada-KV) score importance from an observation window and evict low-scoring tokens, but eviction is irreversible -- so when the importance signal degrades under query-agnostic reuse, accuracy collapses by 11-15 points; uniform low-rank coding keeps every token but spends equal rank everywhere, wasting budget. We observe that both failures share one cure: rank should be allocated, not evicted
